Clinical Reference

Deep Vein Thrombosis & VTE

On this page
Venous thromboembolism (VTE) = a fibrin-rich clot in the deep venous system (DVT) that can embolize to the lungs (PE) — one disease continuum driven by Virchow's triad, treated by interrupting the clotting cascade with anticoagulation.
Proximal vs distal (calf) DVT Provoked vs unprovoked D-dimer + compression US drive the workup Untreated proximal DVT → ~50% embolize; PE fatal in ~10–30% First-line: apixaban / rivaroxaban (DOAC monotherapy) Duration: 3 mo provoked · indefinite if unprovoked/cancer
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story of a clot in the wrong place

A venous thrombus is the right process (hemostasis) happening in the wrong place and at the wrong time. Rudolf Virchow's triad names the three conditions that let it start: venous stasis (immobility, surgery, long travel, heart failure), endothelial injury (trauma, central lines, prior DVT, surgery), and hypercoagulability (cancer, pregnancy/estrogen, inherited thrombophilia, inflammation). Most DVTs nucleate in the low-flow valve pockets of the calf or in the iliofemoral segment, where stagnant blood, local hypoxia, and exposed tissue factor tip the balance toward clotting.

Once tissue factor meets flowing blood, the coagulation cascade fires: factor Xa assembles with factor Va to convert prothrombin into thrombin (IIa); thrombin then cleaves fibrinogen into fibrin and activates platelets, building the fibrin-rich, red-cell-laden "red thrombus" characteristic of veins. Unopposed, the clot propagates proximally. Two things make that dangerous: a fragment can break off and embolize to the lungs (PE), and the clot scars the vein's valves, causing chronic reflux — post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS). Every drug in this guide works by interrupting one specific step in that cascade, or by dissolving fibrin after the fact.

Think of a deep vein as a slow river with one-way lock-gates (valves). When the current stalls (stasis) and the bank is scraped raw (endothelial injury), silt and debris (fibrin + platelets) pile up behind a gate. Anticoagulants don't dig out the pile — they stop new silt from being added so the river's own dredgers (natural fibrinolysis) can slowly clear it. Thrombolytics are the emergency dredger you call when the whole channel is blocked and the land downstream is dying.
Virchow's triad → coagulation cascade → thrombus → embolization/PTS, annotated with exactly where each drug class acts. Red = clotting steps · green = drug targets.
The coagulation cascade — the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge on factor Xa → thrombin → fibrin. DOACs hit Xa or thrombin directly; heparins act through antithrombin; warfarin depletes the vitamin-K-dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X).
Source: Wikimedia Commons — Blood clot formation.svg · Victdomi · CC BY-SA 3.0
Histology of an organizing deep vein thrombus — alternating pale platelet/fibrin and dark red-cell layers ("lines of Zahn") confirm the clot formed in flowing blood ante-mortem.
Source: Wikimedia Commons — Organizing deep vein thrombosis, HE 1.JPG · Patho · CC BY-SA 3.0
The whole guide's through-line: DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) directly inhibit factor Xa; dabigatran and argatroban directly inhibit thrombin (IIa); LMWH/UFH/fondaparinux supercharge antithrombin (UFH inhibits both Xa and IIa; LMWH and fondaparinux mostly Xa); warfarin blocks vitamin-K epoxide reductase, lowering functional factors II, VII, IX, X; and alteplase (tPA) converts plasminogen to plasmin, which lyses existing fibrin. Match the drug to the step and the side effects make sense.
Shared

Presentation & findings — and why

🩺

Symptoms & signs — frequency and the mechanism behind each

DVT findings all flow from one problem: an obstructed deep vein raises pressure and blocks drainage in everything downstream. But signs are notoriously insensitive and non-specific — up to half of DVTs are clinically silent, and the classic exam findings are unreliable, which is exactly why validated scores + objective testing (not gestalt) decide the diagnosis.

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Unilateral leg pain / tenderness~75–85%Venous distension + perivascular inflammation stretch pain fibers along the deep venous course (calf, popliteal fossa, thigh).
Unilateral leg swelling / edema~70–80%Outflow obstruction ↑ hydrostatic pressure upstream → capillary transudation. A >3 cm calf-circumference difference vs the other leg is a Wells criterion.
Warmth of the limb~40–50%Inflammatory hyperemia and increased regional blood volume around the thrombosed segment.
Erythema / discoloration~40%Venous congestion and inflammation; deoxygenated pooled blood gives a dusky/reddish hue.
Dilated superficial (collateral) veins~25–30%Blood reroutes through superficial collaterals when the deep system is blocked — a non-varicose, newly prominent pattern.
Palpable cord~15–30%A thrombosed, firm vein palpable as a tender linear cord along its anatomic course.
Homans' sign (calf pain on dorsiflexion)<15% usefulTraction on the posterior calf veins — neither sensitive nor specific; do not rely on it (classic pimping answer, poor clinical tool).
Phlegmasia cerulea dolens (tense, cyanotic, painful limb)<1%Massive iliofemoral thrombosis obstructs nearly all venous outflow → soaring compartment pressure compromises arterial inflow → limb ischemia/gangrene. A surgical/IR emergency.
Read the patternA unilateral, swollen, painful calf/thigh is DVT until proven otherwise; bilateral leg edema points instead to systemic causes (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, venous insufficiency). No single sign confirms or excludes DVT — that is the entire rationale for the Wells score + D-dimer + ultrasound pathway.
🪛

Imaging findings — the order they appear & the thresholds that matter

Modality / findingWhen / thresholdWhy
Compression ultrasound — non-compressibilityTest of choice (first)The diagnostic sign of DVT: a normal vein collapses fully under probe pressure; a clot-filled vein does not compress. Sensitivity/specificity >95% for proximal (femoral/popliteal) DVT.
Absent respiratory/augmentation flow (Doppler)SupportiveLoss of normal phasic venous flow with respiration/distal compression signals proximal obstruction.
Echogenic intraluminal materialAcute vs chronic clueAcute thrombus is soft, poorly echogenic, and dilates the vein; chronic thrombus is echogenic, retracted, with wall thickening.
Distal (calf) DVT on whole-leg scanIsolated calfLower embolic risk. Options: treat, or serial 2-point US at 1 week to catch proximal propagation (ACCP: image or repeat, individualize).
CT / MR venographyPelvic / IVC / non-diagnostic USReserved for iliac/IVC thrombus, suspected May-Thurner, or when US is limited (obesity, casts). Contrast filling defect confirms.
Contrast venographyHistorical gold standardRarely used now (invasive, contrast load); mainly during catheter-directed intervention.
Compression duplex ultrasound of a deep vein thrombosis — the deep vein fails to collapse under probe pressure and contains echogenic thrombus. This non-compressibility is the diagnostic finding.
Source: Wikimedia Commons — Beheko kaba zain-tronbosia.png · IQmedicine · CC BY-SA 4.0
Ascending contrast venogram showing an intraluminal filling defect (thrombus) in the deep veins of the leg — the historical gold standard, now largely replaced by ultrasound.
Source: Wikimedia Commons — Phlebographie mit Thrombose.jpg · Hellerhoff · CC BY-SA 3.0
A single negative proximal compression ultrasound with a low Wells + negative D-dimer effectively rules out DVT. If Wells is "likely" but US is negative, repeat US in ~1 week (to catch a calf clot propagating proximally) rather than anticoagulating empirically.
🧪

Reading the labs — what each value is telling you

LabWhat it means & why it moves
D-dimerA fibrin degradation product — rises whenever clot is being formed and broken down. High sensitivity, low specificity: a negative D-dimer in a low/intermediate-probability patient safely rules out VTE. Falsely elevated by age, pregnancy, cancer, infection/sepsis, surgery, trauma, hospitalization — so it is a rule-out, never a rule-in. Use the age-adjusted cutoff (age × 10 µg/L for patients >50) to improve specificity in older adults.
CBC — plateletsBaseline before heparin, then trend. A >50% platelet drop 5–10 days into heparin exposure signals HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia) — a prothrombotic emergency requiring immediate heparin cessation and a non-heparin anticoagulant. Baseline thrombocytopenia also shapes bleeding risk and drug choice.
Creatinine / CrClGoverns drug selection and dose. Dabigatran, rivaroxaban, edoxaban are renally cleared (avoid dabigatran if CrCl <30; edoxaban dose-reduce or avoid at CrCl extremes); apixaban is the most renal-friendly DOAC. LMWH accumulates in renal failure — use UFH or anti-Xa-monitored dosing when CrCl <30.
HemoglobinBaseline for bleeding risk; a falling Hb on anticoagulation flags occult bleeding. Unexplained iron-deficiency anemia in an unprovoked VTE can be the first clue to an occult GI malignancy.
PT/INR & aPTTBaseline coagulation before starting therapy. INR titrates warfarin (target 2–3). aPTT (or anti-Xa) titrates a UFH infusion. A prolonged baseline aPTT may hint at a lupus anticoagulant (antiphospholipid syndrome) — relevant because APS changes anticoagulant choice.
Anti-Xa levelDirect measure of heparin effect. Used to titrate UFH (target ~0.3–0.7 IU/mL) when the aPTT is unreliable, and to monitor LMWH in pregnancy, obesity, or renal impairment (peak 4 h post-dose).
LFTsBaseline; severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B/C) is a relative contraindication to DOACs (rivaroxaban contraindicated in Child-Pugh B/C with coagulopathy).
Thrombophilia panelFactor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C/S, antithrombin, antiphospholipid antibodies. Do not send acutely or while on anticoagulation (acute clot and warfarin/heparin distort levels). Test only when it will change duration/management, ideally ≥2 weeks after stopping anticoagulation.
Never send a D-dimer to "confirm" DVT you already suspect strongly — a positive result adds nothing (it's non-specific) and a negative in a high-probability patient doesn't rule it out. In "DVT likely" (Wells ≥2), go straight to ultrasound.
🩺 Clinic — outpatient diagnosis, anticoagulation & duration decisions
Assess

When to suspect & who's at risk

🔍

Outpatient presentation & risk factors

The classic clinic presentation is a unilateral, painful, swollen calf or thigh — often after a provoking event. The job in clinic is to (1) risk-stratify with the Wells score, (2) use D-dimer/ultrasound rationally, and (3) if confirmed, pick an anticoagulant and, crucially, decide how long to treat.

Risk categoryExamplesWhy it matters
Major transient / provokedSurgery >30 min under GA, major trauma, hospitalization/immobility ≥3 days, C-section, leg cast within 3 monthsRisk resolves → 3 months of anticoagulation usually sufficient; low recurrence after stopping.
Minor transientEstrogen (OCP/HRT), pregnancy/postpartum, long-haul travel >8 h, minor surgery, leg injury with reduced mobilityIntermediate recurrence risk; individualize duration.
Persistent / unprovokedActive cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease, unprovoked (no identifiable trigger)High recurrence (~10%/yr, ~30% at 5 yr) → favor extended/indefinite anticoagulation.
Inherited thrombophiliaFactor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C/S or antithrombin deficiencyModestly raises first-event and recurrence risk; rarely changes management alone. Test selectively.
An unprovoked VTE in an adult warrants age/sex-appropriate cancer screening (history, exam, routine bloods, and up-to-date guideline screening) — extensive occult-malignancy CT screening (SOME trial) did not improve outcomes, so screen sensibly, not exhaustively.
Workup

What to order & when

🧪

The Wells → D-dimer → ultrasound pathway

Wells DVT scoreFirst step in every suspected DVT. Stratifies into "unlikely" (≤1) vs "likely" (≥2) to decide whether D-dimer or ultrasound comes next.First
D-dimer (age-adjusted)If Wells "unlikely" (≤1): a negative age-adjusted D-dimer rules out DVT — no imaging. If positive → ultrasound. Do NOT order if Wells "likely."If Wells ≤1
Compression ultrasound (duplex)If Wells "likely" (≥2) OR D-dimer positive. Proximal (2-point) or whole-leg. Non-compressibility = DVT.Confirm
Repeat US in ~1 weekIf Wells "likely" but initial proximal US negative — catches calf DVT propagating proximally.If needed
CBC, CMP (CrCl), PT/INR, aPTTBaseline before anticoagulation — sets drug choice (renal/hepatic function) and gives a bleeding-risk baseline.Baseline
CT/MR venographyOnly for suspected pelvic/IVC thrombus, May-Thurner, or non-diagnostic ultrasound.Selective
Two-tier Wells (ACCP/NICE): ≤1 = DVT unlikely → D-dimer; ≥2 = DVT likely → ultrasound. The interactive Wells calculator is in the Calculators section below.
Treat

Anticoagulation — first-line → escalation

💊

Choosing & dosing the anticoagulant

1
First-line: a DOAC (apixaban or rivaroxaban)
Guideline-preferred over warfarin for most non-cancer VTE — no bridging, no INR monitoring
▾
Apixaban and rivaroxaban directly inhibit factor Xa, choking off thrombin generation at the cascade's convergence point. Apixaban and rivaroxaban are started as monotherapy with a loading phase (no heparin lead-in needed); dabigatran and edoxaban require ≥5 days of parenteral heparin first.
DrugStart (loading)Maintenance → ExtendedWhy it works / notesIf contraindicated / alt
Apixaban10 mg PO BID ×7 days5 mg BID → after 6 mo, 2.5 mg BID for extended prophylaxisDirect Xa inhibitor; most renal-friendly DOAC, lowest major-bleed rate in AMPLIFY. No parenteral lead-in.Rivaroxaban; if DOAC contraindicated → LMWH→warfarin
Rivaroxaban15 mg PO BID ×21 days (with food)20 mg daily → after 6 mo, 10 mg daily for extendedDirect Xa inhibitor; once-daily maintenance aids adherence. Take 15/20 mg with food for absorption.Apixaban (no food requirement, better in CrCl 15–30)
Edoxaban≥5 days parenteral heparin FIRST, then 60 mg daily60 mg daily (30 mg if CrCl 15–50, weight ≤60 kg, or strong P-gp inhibitor)Direct Xa inhibitor, once daily. Requires heparin lead-in (Hokusai-VTE design).Apixaban/rivaroxaban (no lead-in)
Dabigatran≥5 days parenteral heparin FIRST, then 150 mg BID150 mg BID (110 mg BID in EU for age ≥80/bleeding risk)Direct thrombin (IIa) inhibitor; reversible with idarucizumab. Avoid if CrCl <30; dyspepsia common.A Xa-inhibitor DOAC; andexanet reverses Xa agents
Reversal agents: idarucizumab (Praxbind) for dabigatran; andexanet alfa for apixaban/rivaroxaban (4-factor PCC if unavailable); vitamin K + 4-factor PCC for warfarin; protamine for UFH (partial for LMWH).
2
LMWH — cancer, pregnancy, or when a DOAC won't do
Also the parenteral lead-in for edoxaban/dabigatran
▾
LMWH binds antithrombin, accelerating its inactivation of factor Xa (and some IIa). Predictable pharmacokinetics mean no routine monitoring in most patients. Preferred in pregnancy (does not cross the placenta) and historically first-line in cancer (now often replaced by DOACs — see comorbidities).
DrugStartDose / adjustWhy it works / notesIf intolerant / alt
Enoxaparin1 mg/kg SC q12hor 1.5 mg/kg SC daily; if CrCl <30 → 1 mg/kg SC daily; monitor anti-Xa in pregnancy/obesity/renalAntithrombin-mediated anti-Xa. Peak anti-Xa 4 h post-dose (target ~0.6–1.0 IU/mL for q12h dosing).Dalteparin; fondaparinux; UFH if CrCl very low
Dalteparin (cancer)200 IU/kg SC daily ×1 monththen 150 IU/kg daily (CLOT regimen for cancer-associated VTE)The trial-validated LMWH for cancer VTE (CLOT); dose tapers after month 1.Apixaban/edoxaban (Caravaggio/Hokusai-Cancer)
Fondaparinux7.5 mg SC daily (5 mg if <50 kg, 10 mg if >100 kg)Avoid if CrCl <30Synthetic pure anti-Xa pentasaccharide; does not cause HIT — useful as a HIT alternative.Argatroban/bivalirudin if HIT with renal issues
3
Warfarin (VKA) — mechanical valves, APS, severe renal failure, cost
Overlap with parenteral heparin until INR therapeutic ×2 days
▾
Warfarin blocks vitamin-K epoxide reductase, depleting functional factors II, VII, IX, X (and proteins C/S). Because protein C falls first, warfarin is transiently procoagulant — so you must bridge with heparin/LMWH for ≥5 days AND until INR ≥2 for 24 h. Now reserved for situations where DOACs fail or are contraindicated.
DrugStartTitration → TargetWhy it works / notesKey interactions
Warfarin5 mg PO daily (2.5 mg if elderly/frail/liver disease/high bleeding risk)Adjust by INR every few days → INR 2.0–3.0; overlap heparin ≥5 days & until INR ≥2 ×24 hDepletes vitamin-K-dependent factors. Preferred anticoagulant in antiphospholipid syndrome and mechanical valves (DOACs inferior/contraindicated).↑INR: amiodarone, azoles, Bactrim, metronidazole. ↓INR: rifampin, carbamazepine. Diet: leafy greens (vit K).
Duration of therapy3 months for VTE provoked by a major transient risk factor. Extended/indefinite (reassess yearly) for unprovoked proximal DVT/PE, recurrent VTE, active cancer, or antiphospholipid syndrome — provided bleeding risk is acceptable. Distal (calf) DVT: 3 months if treated, or surveillance if low-risk. Reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg BID or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily are options for the extended phase (AMPLIFY-EXT, EINSTEIN-CHOICE).
Monitor

Follow-up & monitoring cadence

📈

What to recheck, and when

On this drugMonitorCadence
Any anticoagulantBleeding, adherence, limb symptoms, recurrenceVisit at ~2–4 weeks, then every 3–6 months
DOACCBC, renal function (CrCl drives dosing)Baseline, then at least annually (more often if CrCl <60 or elderly)
WarfarinINR (target 2–3)Every few days at start → weekly → up to every 4–12 weeks once stable
LMWH (pregnancy/obesity/renal)Anti-Xa peak (4 h post-dose), plateletsPeriodically; platelets days 5–10 for HIT if UFH/LMWH >4 days
AllReassess duration & bleeding-vs-clotting balanceAt 3 months, then annually if extended
At the 3-month mark, actively re-decide: stop (provoked, resolved) vs continue (unprovoked/cancer/APS). Tools like HERDOO2 (women) and the D-dimer after stopping help identify low-recurrence patients who can safely discontinue.
Comorbidities

How comorbidities change management

🔗

The company VTE keeps — and drug interactions

ComorbidityHow it interactsWhat changes
Active cancerHypercoagulable; higher recurrence AND bleeding; drug interactions with chemo.DOAC (apixaban/edoxaban/rivaroxaban) or LMWH acceptable. Caution with edoxaban/rivaroxaban in luminal GI or GU cancers (higher bleeding — Hokusai-Cancer/SELECT-D); apixaban (Caravaggio) had no excess GI bleed. Treat as long as cancer active.
Renal impairmentDOACs and LMWH accumulate.Avoid dabigatran if CrCl <30; apixaban most renal-friendly; edoxaban dose-reduce (30 mg) at CrCl 15–50; LMWH → reduce or use UFH/anti-Xa when CrCl <30. Warfarin/UFH preferred in severe CKD/dialysis.
Pregnancy / postpartumHypercoagulable state; teratogen concerns.LMWH only — warfarin is teratogenic (embryopathy) and DOACs are not recommended (cross placenta, insufficient data). Continue ≥6 weeks postpartum, ≥3 months total.
Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS)Autoimmune hypercoagulability; DOACs underperform.Warfarin (INR 2–3) is preferred — the TRAPS trial showed rivaroxaban caused more arterial thrombosis in triple-positive APS. Avoid DOACs, especially in triple-positive.
ObesityAltered volume of distribution; older concern about DOAC underdosing.Standard-dose apixaban/rivaroxaban now considered acceptable across BMI (ISTH 2021 update); consider anti-Xa checks if using LMWH at extremes.
Liver diseaseCoagulopathy + altered drug metabolism.Rivaroxaban contraindicated in Child-Pugh B/C; use caution/avoid DOACs in significant cirrhosis; LMWH often preferred with careful monitoring.
Prior HITAntibody-mediated, prothrombotic reaction to heparin.Avoid all heparins; use fondaparinux or a DOAC once platelets recover; argatroban/bivalirudin acutely.
Drugs to avoid / use with caution: strong dual P-gp + CYP3A4 inhibitors (azole antifungals like ketoconazole/itraconazole, HIV protease inhibitors, clarithromycin) raise DOAC levels → bleeding; strong inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John's wort, phenobarbital) lower DOAC levels → clot risk (avoid DOACs entirely). Concurrent antiplatelets/NSAIDs compound bleeding — use only with a clear indication. In APS and mechanical valves, DOACs are contraindicated.
Scores

Calculators

🧮

Wells score for DVT — pre-test probability

Stratifies suspected DVT into likely vs unlikely to route the workup. Subtract 2 points if an alternative diagnosis is as likely as DVT.

Active cancer (treatment within 6 mo / palliative) +1
Paralysis, paresis, or recent leg immobilization +1
Bedridden ≥3 days or major surgery within 12 wk +1
Localized tenderness along deep venous system +1
Entire leg swollen +1
Calf swelling >3 cm vs asymptomatic leg +1
Pitting edema confined to symptomatic leg +1
Collateral superficial (non-varicose) veins +1
Previously documented DVT +1
Alternative diagnosis as likely as DVT −2
0
Two-tier interpretation (Wells 2003): ≤1 = DVT unlikely → D-dimer; ≥2 = DVT likely → compression ultrasound. Source: Wells PS et al., NEJM 2003; MDCalc "Wells' Criteria for DVT."
🧮

Wells score for PE — because DVT and PE are one disease

Any DVT patient with dyspnea, chest pain, tachycardia, or hypoxia needs PE risk-stratification. This is the standard (original) Wells PE score.

Clinical signs/symptoms of DVT +3
PE is #1 diagnosis, or equally likely +3
Heart rate >100 +1.5
Immobilization ≥3 days or surgery in prior 4 wk +1.5
Previous DVT/PE +1.5
Hemoptysis +1
Malignancy (treated within 6 mo / palliative) +1
0
Three-tier (original): <2 low, 2–6 moderate, >6 high. Two-tier: ≤4 "PE unlikely" → D-dimer; >4 "PE likely" → CT pulmonary angiography. Source: Wells PS et al., Ann Intern Med 2001; MDCalc.
🔗

Other validated scores — link out (nomograms we won't approximate)

  • Caprini Score (2005) — surgical-patient VTE risk; guides prophylaxis intensity.
  • Padua Prediction Score — medical-inpatient VTE risk (≥4 = high risk → pharmacologic prophylaxis).
  • IMPROVE Bleeding Risk Score — bleeding risk that offsets prophylaxis benefit.
  • HERDOO2 Rule — identifies women with unprovoked VTE who can safely stop anticoagulation.
  • PESI / simplified PESI — PE 30-day mortality & outpatient eligibility (see ICU).
  • Hestia Criteria — outpatient PE treatment eligibility.
Prevent

Prevention & USPSTF context

🛡️

Screening posture for this population

There is no USPSTF recommendation to screen asymptomatic adults for DVT/VTE — diagnosis is symptom- and risk-driven, not screening-based. The relevant USPSTF work is about who not to over-test or over-treat:

GradeRecommendationPopulation
DDo not routinely screen for inherited thrombophilia or use it alone to decide anticoagulation durationAsymptomatic adults; most first-VTE patients (ASH/CHEST guidance)
BProvide VTE prophylaxis assessment (Padua/Caprini) for at-risk hospitalized & surgical patientsMedical & surgical inpatients
—Counsel on modifiable risk: mobilization, hydration on long travel, weigh estrogen-containing contraception in high-risk womenOutpatients with risk factors
The USPSTF did address hormonal contraception + thrombophilia: routine screening before starting estrogen is not recommended, but a personal/strong family history of VTE should steer women toward progestin-only or non-hormonal options.
Escalate

When to refer / admit

🚑

Red flags → ED / admission

Send to ED / admit for: phlegmasia cerulea/alba dolens (tense, discolored, ischemic limb), massive iliofemoral DVT, signs of concurrent PE (dyspnea, chest pain, syncope, hypoxia, tachycardia), high bleeding risk needing monitored anticoagulation, severe pain/limb compromise, or inability to arrange/afford reliable outpatient anticoagulation and follow-up.
Most DVT is outpatientUncomplicated proximal DVT in a hemodynamically stable, adherent patient with no bleeding contraindication is treated at home on a DOAC — no admission needed. Admission is for the exceptions above.
🛏️ Wards — inpatient anticoagulation, prophylaxis & the diagnostic triage
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria & the diagnostic algorithm

Most DVT is managed outpatient. Admit only when there's a limb threat, a bleeding/therapeutic problem, or a need for a procedure:

  • Extensive iliofemoral DVT or phlegmasia cerulea/alba dolens (limb-threatening).
  • Concurrent symptomatic PE, especially intermediate/high-risk.
  • Active bleeding or high bleeding risk requiring monitored anticoagulation.
  • Severe renal failure (CrCl <30) complicating anticoagulant choice.
  • Cannot manage outpatient — uncontrolled pain, poor support, unable to obtain/self-administer drug, unreliable follow-up.
  • Candidate for advanced therapy — catheter-directed thrombolysis, thrombectomy, or IVC filter.
The end-to-end DVT triage: Wells → D-dimer/ultrasound → confirm → outpatient DOAC vs ICU-level intervention for limb-threatening clot.

Acute inpatient anticoagulation

💊

Therapeutic anticoagulation + the UFH nomogram

1
Start therapeutic anticoagulation immediately
DOAC or LMWH for most; UFH infusion when a procedure, bleeding risk, or CrCl <30 is in play
▾
Same cascade targets as clinic: pick the agent whose pharmacology fits the patient's kidneys, bleeding risk, and likelihood of needing rapid reversal. In the hospital, favor UFH when you may need to turn anticoagulation off quickly (procedure, high bleeding risk) because of its short half-life and protamine reversibility.
AgentStartTitration / adjustWhy it works / notesAlt
Apixaban / rivaroxabanApix 10 mg BID ×7d; Riva 15 mg BID ×21dthen apix 5 mg BID / riva 20 mg dailyDirect Xa inhibitors; start at admission, no heparin lead-in — simplest inpatient-to-home transition.LMWH → warfarin bridge
Enoxaparin (therapeutic)1 mg/kg SC q12h1 mg/kg SC daily if CrCl <30; anti-Xa in obesity/pregnancy/renalAntithrombin-mediated anti-Xa; predictable, good bridge to warfarin or lead-in for edoxaban/dabigatran.UFH if CrCl very low
UFH IV infusionBolus 80 units/kg, then 18 units/kg/hrTitrate to aPTT 1.5–2.5× control or anti-Xa 0.3–0.7 IU/mL; recheck 6 h after start & each rate changeBoosts antithrombin against Xa & IIa; short half-life + protamine-reversible — ideal when bleeding/procedure risk or CrCl <30.Argatroban/bivalirudin if HIT
Warfarin (bridge)5 mg PO daily (2.5 mg if frail/elderly/liver)INR 2–3; overlap heparin ≥5 days AND until INR ≥2 ×24 hVKA; for APS, mechanical valve, severe renal failure, or DOAC contraindication.DOAC if eligible
When the home/prior anticoagulant dose is unknown or was recently taken, default to a therapeutic UFH infusion (titratable, reversible) rather than stacking a full LMWH/DOAC dose on top of unknown residual drug — then reassess timing and renal function before committing to a definitive agent.

Padua ≥4 (medical) / Caprini (surgical) → prophylactic, NOT therapeutic, dosing
▾
Every admitted patient gets a VTE-risk assessment. This is the flip side of the disease: preventing the clot you're treating in the next bed. Prophylactic doses are lower than treatment doses.

What to trend each day

📈

Daily assessment targets

TrendWhy / threshold
CBC / plateletsA ≥50% platelet drop on day 4–14 of heparin → suspect HIT (score 4Ts); watch Hgb for occult bleeding.
Renal functionRe-dose DOAC/LMWH as CrCl shifts; a falling CrCl may force a switch to UFH.
Bleeding assessmentSites, Hgb trend, occult blood, neuro checks — the balance against clot protection.
Limb examCircumference, color (new cyanosis → phlegmasia), pain, capillary refill, distal pulses/sensation.
Anticoagulation levelaPTT/anti-Xa (UFH, 6 h after each change), INR (warfarin bridge) — confirm you're in-range.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers (concrete)

Transfer to ICU for: developing phlegmasia cerulea dolens (worsening cyanosis, tense swelling, loss of pulses/sensation) → limb-threatening; hemodynamic instability from concurrent PE (SBP <90 or a drop ≥40 mmHg for >15 min, or new vasopressor need); major bleeding requiring transfusion/reversal; or need for catheter-directed thrombolysis, thrombectomy, or systemic lysis.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: pain controlled, limb stable/improving, on a definitive anticoagulant the patient can obtain and self-administer, renal function stable, no active bleeding, and follow-up (plus an INR plan if on warfarin) arranged. Deliver anticoagulation counseling and a written duration plan (3 months vs extended).

Home

Stable, independent, reliable with oral DOAC and follow-up — the default for uncomplicated DVT.

Home health

Needs teaching/observation for LMWH self-injection or has limited mobility; nurse visits for education.

SNF

Deconditioned after a prolonged admission; needs 24h skilled nursing, <3h therapy/day.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Post-phlegmasia/ischemic limb needing intensive rehab, ≥3h therapy/day, ≥2 disciplines.

LTAC

Prolonged complex care (e.g., ventilator weaning after massive PE) >25 days.

Hospice / palliative

Advanced cancer VTE with comfort-focused goals; weigh anticoagulation burden vs benefit.
🫀 ICU — limb-threatening clot, thrombolysis & HIT
Admit

ICU triggers & severe presentations

🚨

When DVT belongs in the unit

Phlegmasia cerulea dolens — massive multilevel iliofemoral occlusion obstructs nearly all venous outflow → soaring compartment pressure compromises arterial inflow → limb ischemia and venous gangrene. Anticoagulate immediately (UFH infusion), elevate the limb, aggressively fluid-resuscitate (large volumes sequester in the swollen limb), and get urgent IR/vascular for thrombus removal.
Severe presentationWhat it is / ICU action
Phlegmasia cerulea dolensTense, cyanotic, painful limb; threatened. UFH + elevation + fluids + urgent thrombus removal (CDT/thrombectomy ± surgery).
Phlegmasia alba dolensPale, swollen, painful (reflex arterial spasm); often precedes cerulea. Same aggressive anticoagulation + IR pathway.
Massive iliofemoral DVTHigh clot burden, severe-PTS/embolic risk; candidate for catheter-directed therapy in low-bleeding-risk patients.
Concurrent massive/submassive PEHemodynamic instability → PE high-risk pathway (systemic thrombolysis, RV support) — see companion PE reference.
Major bleeding on anticoagulationReversal (idarucizumab / andexanet / PCC / protamine), transfusion, source control.
Massive proximal DVT producing gross unilateral swelling and discoloration — the clinical extreme that, if outflow fails entirely, becomes phlegmasia cerulea dolens.
Source: Wikimedia Commons — Deep vein thrombosis of the right leg.jpg · James Heilman, MD · CC BY-SA 3.0
Deep venous anatomy of the lower limb — iliofemoral (common femoral/iliac) thrombosis carries the highest burden and the greatest phlegmasia/PTS risk.
Source: Wikimedia Commons — 2136ab Lower Limb Veins Anterior Posterior.jpg · OpenStax College · CC BY 3.0
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Serial limb exams + compartment monitoring in phlegmasia — circumference, color, pulses, sensation, capillary refill; watch for reperfusion syndrome after thrombus removal.
  • Avoid placing new lines in the affected/thrombosed limb.
  • Continuous telemetry + pulse oximetry if concurrent PE; arterial line/central access as shock dictates.
  • Trend CBC/platelets (HIT + bleeding), fibrinogen if lytic therapy running (hold/adjust if <150 mg/dL), renal/hepatic function (drives argatroban vs bivalirudin), and the anticoagulation level (aPTT/anti-Xa).
Reperfuse

Thrombus-removal & lytic therapy

💉

Which intervention, why, and the dosing

Anticoagulants stop clot growth; they do not dissolve it. When a limb is threatened, you need active fibrinolysis — alteplase (tPA) converts plasminogen to plasmin, which actively degrades the fibrin mesh. Delivering it into the clot (catheter-directed) concentrates the lytic effect while limiting systemic bleeding.
InterventionMechanismDosing / approachEffectWhen to pick
Catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT)Intrathrombus plasminogen→plasminLow-dose alteplase infused via multi-side-hole catheter over hours (institution protocol)Dissolves clot locally, restores outflowIliofemoral DVT with severe symptoms / limb threat, low bleeding risk
Pharmacomechanical CDTLysis + device maceration/aspirationAdds mechanical clot disruption to shorten lytic exposureFaster clearance, less lytic doseWhen you want to limit lytic time/bleeding
Percutaneous mechanical/aspiration thrombectomyDevice-based clot removal± low-dose lyticRemoves clot without full lysisLysis contraindicated (recent surgery/bleed)
Systemic thrombolysisSystemic plasmin activationAlteplase 100 mg IV over 2 h (accelerated 0.6 mg/kg over 15 min, max 50 mg, in arrest)High bleeding riskOnly if no catheter access & limb/life threatened
Surgical venous thrombectomyOpen clot extractionOperativeDefinitive when endovascular failsPhlegmasia with impending gangrene, endovascular unavailable
CDT does NOT prevent PTS in routine proximal DVT. ATTRACT (2017): pharmacomechanical CDT gave no PTS reduction (47% vs 48%) and more major bleeding (1.7% vs 0.3%). But CaVenT showed a durable benefit specifically in iliofemoral DVT (5-yr PTS 43% vs 71%, ARR 28%). Reserve CDT for extensive iliofemoral DVT with severe symptoms or limb threat in low-bleeding-risk patients — not every proximal clot.
HIT / Filter

HIT & IVC filters

🧫

Non-heparin anticoagulants & when to filter

Suspect HIT when platelets fall ≥50% (or below 150k) on day 4–14 of any heparin exposure (or within 1 day if recent exposure), ± new thrombosis. Score the 4Ts; if intermediate/high → STOP all heparin (including flushes and LMWH), send HIT antibody/serotonin-release assay, and start a non-heparin anticoagulant. Do NOT transfuse platelets unless bleeding; do NOT start warfarin until platelets recover (venous limb gangrene risk).
AgentStartTitration / adjustWhy / clearanceAlt
Argatroban2 mcg/kg/min IV (no bolus)0.5–1.2 mcg/kg/min if hepatic dysfunction/HF/post-cardiac-surgery/critically ill; titrate aPTT 1.5–3× baseline (<100 s)Direct thrombin inhibitor; hepatically cleared → use in renal failure. Prolongs INR (complicates warfarin overlap).Bivalirudin
Bivalirudin~0.15 mg/kg/hr IV (no bolus for HIT)Titrate aPTT 1.5–2.5×Direct thrombin inhibitor; part-renal/part-enzymatic clearance → useful in combined hepatic + renal impairment.Argatroban
Fondaparinux5 mg (<50 kg) / 7.5 mg (50–100 kg) / 10 mg (>100 kg) SC dailyAvoid if CrCl <30Pure anti-Xa; does not cause HIT. For stable HIT; no routine monitoring.DOAC once stable
DOAC (apixaban/rivaroxaban)Standard VTE dosingOnce platelets recoveringASH 2018 endorses DOACs for clinically stable HIT — convenient transition.Fondaparinux

IVC filter — narrow indications

Place a filter only for an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation in a patient with acute proximal DVT/PE, or recurrent VTE despite therapeutic anticoagulation (true failure). Filters do not treat clot and do not replace anticoagulation — resume anticoagulation as soon as safe and retrieve retrievable filters promptly. Routine filter + anticoagulation is not recommended (PREPIC2: no reduction in recurrent PE, late increase in DVT).

An inferior vena cava (IVC) filter — a mechanical net that catches emboli. A bridge for patients who cannot be anticoagulated, not a substitute for it; retrieve when anticoagulation can resume.
Source: Wikimedia Commons — 3D Medical Animation Inferior Vena Filter.jpg · https://www.scientificanimations.com · CC BY-SA 4.0
Rescue

Refractory / adjuncts

⚙️

When first steps aren't enough

  • Fasciotomy for compartment syndrome complicating phlegmasia after reperfusion.
  • Surgical thrombectomy when endovascular therapy fails or is unavailable in a threatened limb.
  • Major-bleed reversal: idarucizumab (dabigatran), andexanet alfa or 4-factor PCC (Xa-inhibitors), vitamin K + PCC (warfarin), protamine (UFH; partial for LMWH).
  • Concurrent high-risk PE: systemic thrombolysis, catheter embolectomy, or VA-ECMO per the PE pathway.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Step down when: limb perfusion secured and improving (resolving cyanosis, intact pulses/sensation), hemodynamically stable off vasopressors, no active/major bleeding, on stable therapeutic anticoagulation, platelets stable/recovering (if HIT), and any procedure (CDT/thrombectomy/filter) completed with a stable post-procedure course. Not yet if the limb exam is still worsening, lytic infusion is ongoing, or platelets are still falling.

Sources, trials & guidelines

Major guidelines

  • CHEST 2021 — Stevens SM et al. Antithrombotic Therapy for VTE Disease. journal.chestnet.org (duration, DOAC-first, distal-DVT serial imaging, IVC filter, catheter therapy).
  • ASH 2020 — Ortel TL et al. Management of VTE: treatment of DVT and PE. Blood Advances. ashpublications.org
  • ASH 2018 — Cuker A et al. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) guidelines. PMC6258919
  • ESC 2019 — Acute PE Guidelines (Eur Heart J) — risk stratification, UFH nomogram, thrombolysis dosing. academic.oup.com
  • CHEST 2016 — Kearon C et al. (provoked/unprovoked framework). journal.chestnet.org

Landmark trials

Trial (year)ResultWhy it matters
AMPLIFY (2013)Apixaban recurrent VTE 2.3% vs 2.7% (warfarin); major bleed 0.6% vs 1.8%. PMID 23808982Oral apixaban, no lead-in, less bleeding → first-line.
EINSTEIN-DVT/PE (2010/12)Rivaroxaban non-inferior; single-drug, no parenteral lead-in. PMID 21128814Established single-oral-drug DVT therapy.
RE-COVER (2009)Dabigatran (after ≥5 d heparin) recurrent VTE 2.4% vs 2.1%. PMID 19940300Direct thrombin inhibitor validated; needs heparin lead-in.
Hokusai-VTE (2013)Edoxaban (after heparin) non-inferior 3.2% vs 3.5%, less bleeding. PMID 23991658Once-daily edoxaban; heparin lead-in required.
CLOT (2003)Dalteparin recurrence 8.0% vs 15.8% (warfarin) in cancer. PMID 12853587Made LMWH the cancer-VTE standard (now often DOAC).
Caravaggio (2020)Apixaban non-inferior to dalteparin (5.6% vs 7.9%) without excess major bleed. PMID 32223112Preferred oral option for cancer VTE.
Hokusai-VTE Cancer (2018)Edoxaban non-inferior (7.9% vs 11.3%) but ↑ GI bleed (6.9% vs 4.0%). PMID 29231094Avoid edoxaban/rivaroxaban in luminal GI cancer.
AMPLIFY-EXT (2013)Apixaban 2.5 or 5 mg BID vs placebo: recurrence 1.7% vs 8.8%, no ↑ major bleed. NEJMValidated reduced-dose extended therapy.
EINSTEIN-CHOICE (2017)Riva 10 or 20 mg daily both > aspirin 100 mg for recurrence, similar bleeding. PMID 28316279Low-dose rivaroxaban for extended prevention beats aspirin.
ATTRACT (2017)Pharmacomechanical CDT: no PTS reduction (47% vs 48%), ↑ major bleed (1.7% vs 0.3%). NEJMCDT not for routine proximal DVT.
CaVenT (2012/16)Iliofemoral DVT: additional CDT cut 5-yr PTS 43% vs 71% (ARR 28%). Lancet HaematolSupports CDT in selected extensive iliofemoral DVT.
PREPIC2 (2015)Filter + anticoagulation did NOT reduce recurrent PE vs anticoagulation alone. PMID 25919526IVC filters are not a substitute for anticoagulation.
TRAPS (2018)Rivaroxaban caused excess arterial thrombosis in triple-positive APS (stopped early). PMID 30030299Use warfarin, NOT DOACs, in antiphospholipid syndrome.
CALISTO (2010)Fondaparinux 2.5 mg ×45 d cut symptomatic VTE/extension ~85% in SVT. PMID 20860504Treat significant superficial vein thrombosis.
REVERSE II (HERDOO2) (2017)Women with score 0–1 safely stopped anticoagulation (3.0%/yr recurrence). BMJ / PMCIdentifies low-risk women who can discontinue.
ADJUST-PE (2014)Age-adjusted D-dimer (age×10 if >50) safely raised the cutoff, cut imaging. PMID 24643601Fewer unnecessary scans in older patients.
